newsitem.title: SAUDI ARABIA: Mitsubishi signs $1.1 bln Saudi power deal.
newsitem.headline: Mitsubishi signs $1.1 bln Saudi power deal.

text.p: Mitsubishi Heavy Industries of Japan on Tuesday signed a 4.155 billion riyal ($1.11 billion) deal to build a new power plant for Saudi Consolidated Electric Company - East (SCECO-East).
SCECO-East Chairman Faheid Fahd al-Shareef said his company would finance the 2,400-megawatt Ghazlan II power plant from its own resources and a $500 million bank loan.
He told reporters after the signing ceremony at SCECO-East's headquarters in Dammam that the ten-year loan was expected to be signed with five regional and international banks in December.
The signing of the contract formalised a letter of intent SCECO-East awarded Mitsubishi in July.

The company has accepted an offer from Al Bank Al Saudi Al Fransi, known as Saudi French Bank, Chase Investment Bank of Chase Manhattan, National Commercial Bank, Gulf International Bank and Saudi British Bank to provide the loan.

Saudi Industry and Electricity Minister Hashem bin Abdullah bin Hashem Yamani said in a statement the loan "has been offered at very reasonable conditions, which testifies to confidence in the Saudi economy."
"This loan is considered among the best commercial loans offered to a Saudi company and proves the credit-worthiness of SCECO-East," Shareef said.

Officials said the new plant consists of four units, each with a capacity of 600 megawatts. The first is expected to come on stream in December 1999, the second in February 2000, the third in February 2001 and the fourth in February 2002.
The plant is part of a plan to raise power generation in the kingdom to 60,000 megawatts over 25 years from 19,000 megawatts now, officials said.
Shareef said SCECO-East has projects worth 2 billion riyals to integrate the new power plant into the main power system and to set up transmission lines and substations.
He said integrating the plant would cost around one billion riyals and would be put up for bidding within a year.
Under the contract, Mitsubishi will have to train Saudis who will operate and maintain the plant once it is handed over.

Officials said Saudi Arabia has invited bids for a 1,750 megawatt power plant in Shuaiba. They declined to give the cost but said it was likely contractors awarded the project would have to finance it.
